blocks.recap_md: Lisp began as McCarthy's formalism for recursion equations in the late 1950s but evolved informally into a family of dialects; the dialect used in this book is Scheme.
Lisp was historically inefficient for numerical computation but is used here because procedures can themselves be represented and manipulated as data.

knowledge_items.statement: Lisp began as a mathematical formalism (McCarthy, late 1950s) but became a practical, informally-evolved family of dialects; the dialect used in this book is Scheme.

The book uses Lisp because Lisp procedures can themselves be represented and manipulated as data, blurring the usual distinction between 'passive' data and 'active' processes - a capability central to techniques explored later in the book.

questions.prompt: Which specific dialect of Lisp does this book (SICP) use?
questions.explanation: The text states directly: Lisp is by now a family of dialects, and the dialect of Lisp used in this book is called Scheme.

questions.prompt: What key property of Lisp does the text say makes it especially well-suited for the book's discussion of programming?
options: Lisp procedures (descriptions of processes) can themselves be represented and manipulated as Lisp data, blurring the usual distinction between passive data and active processes
Lisp historically had the fastest numerical performance of any programming language
Lisp requires no punctuation of any kind, making programs easier to type
Lisp was the very first programming language ever created, predating Fortran
questions.explanation: The text names this as the most significant feature: Lisp descriptions of processes (procedures) can themselves be represented and manipulated as data - not raw performance (Lisp was historically slower than Fortran for numerics) and not being the oldest language (Fortran is older).
